explanations.explanation: Right on the money, baker. Job says, "Iron is taken from the earth, and copper is smelted from ore." (Job 28:2) So the metals come out of the ground, same as my flour comes out of a bag I swear I closed. Digging is the whole business here.

I see why the sea came to mind, baker, since Job talks about water later on. But here he says, "Iron is taken from the earth." (Job 28:2) Nobody is fishing for iron with a net. Copper comes from ore, and the ore is in the ground.

Iron falling out of the sky would make for a very rough Tuesday, friend. Job says, "Iron is taken from the earth, and copper is smelted from ore." (Job 28:2) You have to dig for it. Look down, not up.

That's right, baker. Job says, "Man puts an end to the darkness; he probes the farthest recesses for ore in deepest darkness." (Job 28:3) The miner goes where it's darkest and keeps going. That's a whole lot of nerve for a little ore.
This one is in the text, friend. Job says, "Man puts an end to the darkness." (Job 28:3) The miner pushes into the farthest recesses looking for ore, in deepest darkness. So the statement is true.

You've got it, baker. Job says, "Far from human habitation he cuts a shaft in places forgotten by the foot of man." (Job 28:4) No neighbors, no foot traffic, nobody waving hello. Just the miner and his shaft.

A mine by the city gate would be a loud neighbor, friend. Job says the shaft is cut "Far from human habitation… in places forgotten by the foot of man." (Job 28:4) That's the opposite of a gate. This miner works where nobody walks.

Busy roads are exactly where this miner is not, baker. Job says he cuts the shaft "Far from human habitation… in places forgotten by the foot of man." (Job 28:4) Forgotten by feet means no traffic at all. Too many people on the road, not enough ore.

Baked right, baker! Job says, "Its rocks are the source of sapphires, containing flecks of gold." (Job 28:6) Two treasures in one spot. That's like finding chocolate chips AND a second batch of chocolate chips.

Pearls are a fair guess for treasure, but Job keeps this one underground, friend. He says, "Its rocks are the source of sapphires, containing flecks of gold." (Job 28:6) The treasure is in the rocks, not in the water. Sapphires and gold, that's the prize.

Nice stones, baker, but they're not the ones on Job's list here. He says, "Its rocks are the source of sapphires, containing flecks of gold." (Job 28:6) The rocks hold sapphires, and the gold comes in flecks. Keep your eye on the blue ones.
Careful, baker, this one is tricky. Job says, "Proud beasts have never trodden it; no lion has ever prowled over it." (Job 28:8) So no lion has been on that path. The statement is false.
That's right, baker. Job says, "Proud beasts have never trodden it; no lion has ever prowled over it." (Job 28:8) Not the falcon, not the lion. The king of the jungle never made it down that path.

You've got it, baker. Job says the miner "hews out channels in the rocks, and his eyes spot every treasure." (Job 28:10) Down in the dark, he still sees what's valuable. I can't even spot my own spatula on a clean counter.
Job says it plainly, friend. The miner "hews out channels in the rocks, and his eyes spot every treasure." (Job 28:10) His eyes catch every treasure down there. So the statement is true.

Yes, baker! The miner stops up the streams "to bring what is hidden to light." (Job 28:11) Hidden things dragged out into the open. I know a little something about being hidden and then brought into the light.

Ruin sounds dramatic, friend, but that's not what Job says. The miner stops up the sources of the streams "to bring what is hidden to light." (Job 28:11) The goal is finding treasure, not wrecking things. Hidden things come out into the light.
Stopping up a stream does sound wasteful, baker. But Job says the miner does it "to bring what is hidden to light." (Job 28:11) The treasure was hidden, and he wants it seen. Light is the word.

Right, baker. Job says, "No man can know its value, nor is it found in the land of the living." (Job 28:13) We just heard about all that silver and gold, and wisdom is worth more than any of it. Nobody can put a price tag on it.

Close, friend, but that's not the word. Job says, "No man can know its value." (Job 28:13) He's talking about what wisdom is worth, not where it starts. After all the treasure talk, value is the point.
Wisdom has no end in sight, baker, but that's not what Job says. He says, "No man can know its value." (Job 28:13) After all that talk of silver and gold, he's talking about worth. The word is value.
I get the thought, baker, but Job says the opposite. "No man can know its value, nor is it found in the land of the living." (Job 28:13) Wisdom isn't found there. The statement is false.
Right, baker. Job says wisdom "is not found in the land of the living." (Job 28:13) You can't just wander around and bump into it. Hang on, because Job has more to say about where it is.
I'd love for it to be that easy, baker. But Job says, "It cannot be bought with gold, nor can its price be weighed out in silver." (Job 28:15) No amount of gold gets it. The statement is false.
Correct, baker. Job says, "It cannot be bought with gold, nor can its price be weighed out in silver." (Job 28:15) You can't pay for it, no matter how big the pile. Wisdom doesn't take cash.

explanations.answer: They've heard a rumor about it
explanations.explanation: You've got it, baker. Job says, "Abaddon and Death say, 'We have heard a rumor about it.'" (Job 28:22) Abaddon is a name for the place of destruction. Even they only caught a whisper.
Nobody's holding a key in this verse, friend. Job says, "Abaddon and Death say, 'We have heard a rumor about it.'" (Job 28:22) They don't have it. They only heard a rumor.

Almost, baker, but they did hear something. Job says, "Abaddon and Death say, 'We have heard a rumor about it.'" (Job 28:22) Abaddon is a name for the place of destruction. A rumor is more than nothing, but it's still not the real thing.
That's it, baker! Job says, "But God understands its way, and He knows its place." (Job 28:23) Everything else came up empty, and then comes the big turn. God knows.
Good guess, friend, but that's not the word. Job says, "But God understands its way, and He knows its place." (Job 28:23) The point is that God knows where wisdom is. Understands is the answer.
Sealing is more my department, baker, since I seal cookie boxes. Job says, "But God understands its way, and He knows its place." (Job 28:23) It's about what God knows. The word is understands.

explanations.answer: He sees everything under the heavens
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. Job says, "For He looks to the ends of the earth and sees everything under the heavens." (Job 28:24) Nothing is out of His sight. That's why He knows where wisdom is.

explanations.answer: He has stored it in the heavens
explanations.explanation: That's a nice picture, friend, but Job doesn't say it. He says, "For He looks to the ends of the earth and sees everything under the heavens." (Job 28:24) The reason God knows is that He sees everything. Storing it isn't in the verse.

explanations.answer: He hid it away there Himself
explanations.explanation: Job never says that, baker. He says, "For He looks to the ends of the earth and sees everything under the heavens." (Job 28:24) The reason is what God sees. Nothing is said about hiding it.

explanations.answer: He looked at it and established it
explanations.explanation: Right, baker. Job says, "then He looked at wisdom and appraised it; He established it and searched it out." (Job 28:27) This happened right when God set up the wind, the waters and the rain. Wisdom was part of the picture.

explanations.answer: He divided it among the nations
explanations.explanation: No nations show up in this verse, friend. Job says, "then He looked at wisdom and appraised it; He established it and searched it out." (Job 28:27) God looked at it and established it. Dividing isn't in the text.

explanations.answer: He poured it out with the rain
explanations.explanation: The rain is in the verse before, baker, but wisdom isn't poured out with it. Job says, "then He looked at wisdom and appraised it; He established it and searched it out." (Job 28:27) God looked at it and established it. The rain is just the timing.
That's it, baker. Job says God told man, "Behold, the fear of the Lord, that is wisdom." (Job 28:28) After all that digging and searching, the answer was right there. No shovel needed.
Elders can be a blessing, friend, but that's not what God says. Job says God told man, "Behold, the fear of the Lord, that is wisdom." (Job 28:28) Wisdom is the fear of the Lord. That's the answer.

A lot of learning is a good thing, baker, but it's not the answer here. Job says God told man, "Behold, the fear of the Lord, that is wisdom." (Job 28:28) Wisdom is the fear of the Lord. Not a library, not a diploma.

You've got it, baker. God says, "and to turn away from evil is understanding." (Job 28:28) So wisdom is the fear of the Lord, and understanding is turning away from evil. Two short lines, and that's the whole answer.
This one is right there in the verse, friend. God says, "and to turn away from evil is understanding." (Job 28:28) So the statement is true. Understanding is turning away from evil.
